introduction_markdown:
Multiple choice paper (0780 Physics 1, June 2019, Advanced Level, one and a half hours). Answer ALL 50 questions; all questions carry equal marks. Each question has FOUR suggested answers A, B, C and D; mark only one answer for each question (if you mark more than one you score zero). Mobile phones are NOT allowed in the examination room. Calculators and Formulae booklets are allowed.

**Constants used in the answers** (the paper itself prints no data sheet): acceleration of free fall $g = 9.8\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$ (this is the value that gives the printed $392\ \mathrm{W}$ of question 44); speed of light $c = 3.00\times10^{8}\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$; Planck constant $h = 6.63\times10^{-34}\ \mathrm{J\,s}$; elementary charge $e = 1.60\times10^{-19}\ \mathrm{C}$; electron mass $m_e = 9.11\times10^{-31}\ \mathrm{kg}$; $\mu_0 = 4\pi\times10^{-7}\ \mathrm{H\,m^{-1}}$.
enonce_intro_markdown:
**Section I (thirty five questions), Questions 1-35.** Directions: Each of the thirty five questions or incomplete statements in this section is followed by four suggested answers. Select the best answer in each case.

**Section II (ten questions), Multiple Selection, Questions 36-45.** Directions: for each group of questions below ONE or TWO of the responses given is/are correct. Choose: A - if 1 and 2 are correct; B - if 2 and 3 are correct; C - if 1 only is correct; D - if 3 only is correct. (Directions summarised: A = 1, 2 only; B = 2, 3 only; C = 1 only; D = 3 only.)

**Section III (five questions), Questions 46-50.** Directions: Each of the questions (46-50) has four sets of graphs A-D. Which of the graphs in each question best fits the relationship between $x$ and $y$?

questions.enonce_markdown: Which of the following statements best explains why the homogeneity of a physical equation is not a sufficient condition for the correctness of the equation?
questions.corrige_markdown:
A homogeneity check compares only the **units (dimensions)** of the terms. It cannot see a dimensionless number, so an equation can be homogeneous and still wrong. Example: $E_k = mv^2$ is homogeneous (both sides in J) but the correct equation is $E_k = \tfrac12 mv^2$.

Option C gives exactly this reason. A only defines homogeneity. B states the conclusion ("necessary but not sufficient") without giving the reason. D describes a use of the test, not its limitation. **Answer: C.**

choix.texte: For an equation to be homogenous the units of the physical quantities on both sides of the equation must be equal.
All correct equations are homogenous but not all homogenous equations are correct.
A homogenous equation may contain a wrong unit less constant.
Homogeneity can be used to test the relationship between quantities in a physical equation.

questions.enonce_markdown:
Which of the following sets $X$, $Y$ and $Z$ contains two vector quantities and one scalar quantity?

| | X | Y | Z |
|---|---|---|---|
| A | Power | velocity | E-Field |
| B | Force | Energy | Pressure |
| C | Weight | Momentum | Displacement |
| D | Mass | Torque | Temperature |
questions.corrige_markdown:
Vectors have magnitude and direction: velocity, electric field, force, weight, momentum, displacement, torque. Scalars have magnitude only: power, energy, pressure (the force per unit area acts equally in all directions), mass, temperature.

- A: power (scalar), velocity (vector), E-field (vector): two vectors and one scalar.
- B: one vector (force). C: three vectors. D: one vector (torque).

**Answer: A.**

questions.enonce_markdown: A small mass $m$ is suspended from one end of a vertical string and then whirled in a horizontal circle at a constant velocity $v$.
questions.corrige_markdown:
This is a conical pendulum. Two forces act on the mass: its weight $mg$ (down) and the tension $T$ along the string, which makes an angle $\theta$ with the vertical.

- Vertical (no vertical acceleration): $T\cos\theta = mg$.
- Horizontal (centripetal force towards the centre of the circle): $T\sin\theta = \dfrac{mv^2}{r}$.

Dividing: $\tan\theta = \dfrac{v^2}{rg}$, which is option D. A is wrong (the centripetal force is $T\sin\theta$), B is wrong (the tension also acts), C is wrong (the weight is balanced by $T\cos\theta$). **Answer: D.**

choix.texte: The centripetal force acting on $m$ is $T\cos\theta$
The only force on $m$ is its weight.
The weight of the mas is given by $T\sin\theta$
The string become inclined to the vertical at an angle $\theta$ where $\tan\theta = v^2/rg$

questions.enonce_markdown: An iron ball $X$ and a copper ball $Y$ of the same volume are thrown horizontally with the same velocity $u$ from the top of a tall building. Which of the following statements is true if air resistance is ignored?
questions.corrige_markdown: Without air resistance the only force is the weight, so the acceleration is $g$ for both balls whatever their mass (the masses differ because iron is denser than copper, but the mass cancels). The vertical motion is identical, so the time of fall is the same, $t=\sqrt{2h/g}$. The horizontal velocity $u$ is constant, so both land at the same horizontal distance $ut$. **Answer: D.**

choix.texte: X reaches the ground before y at the same distance from the building
X reaches the ground at the same time with y but at a smaller distance from the building.
X reaches the ground at the same time with y but at a greater distance from the building.
X and y reach the ground at the same time and at the same distance from the building.

questions.enonce_markdown: A snooker ball $x$ collides head-on with another snooker ball $y$ moving in the opposite direction. Which of the following statements below is the correct statement of the conservation of momentum?
questions.corrige_markdown:
Principle of conservation of momentum: in a collision with no external resultant force, the **total momentum of the system** (the two balls together) is the same before and after.

- A is the only statement of this principle (the total momentum of $x$ and $y$ stays constant).
- B is false: each ball exerts an impulse on the other, so the momentum of $x$ alone changes.
- C is true only if the total momentum happens to be zero.
- D has no basis: the final momenta depend on the masses and speeds.

**Answer: A.**

choix.texte: The total momentum in the x and y directions stay constant.
The initial and final momenta of x is the same.
The sum of the x and y components of the momentum is zero.
The final momentum of x is the same as the final momentum of y.

questions.enonce_markdown: A battery is connected to a parallel-plate capacitor that stores $6.0\times10^{-4}\ \mathrm{J}$ of energy. If the separation between the plates of the capacitor is doubled, which of the following would be the value of the energy stored?
questions.corrige_markdown:
The battery stays connected, so the p.d. $V$ across the plates is constant. The capacitance $C=\dfrac{\varepsilon_0 A}{d}$ is halved when $d$ is doubled. The stored energy $E=\tfrac12 CV^2$ is therefore halved:

$E' = \dfrac{6.0\times10^{-4}}{2} = 3.0\times10^{-4}\ \mathrm{J}$.

(If the battery had been disconnected, the charge would stay constant and the energy $Q^2/2C$ would double instead.) **Answer: C.**

questions.enonce_markdown:
![fig-1](gce-al-physics-2019-p1-officiel-cameroun_exercice_1_fig_1.png)

Figure 1 shows a battery of $12\ \mathrm{V}$ connected to three resistors. Which of the following sets of values is the correct value of the p.d. across $XY$ and main current in the circuit?
questions.corrige_markdown:
The $6\ \Omega$ and $3\ \Omega$ resistors are in parallel between $X$ and $Y$:

$R_{XY} = \dfrac{6\times3}{6+3} = 2\ \Omega$.

This is in series with the $4\ \Omega$ resistor: $R_{total} = 2+4 = 6\ \Omega$.

Main current: $I = \dfrac{12}{6} = 2\ \mathrm{A}$. P.d. across $XY$: $V_{XY} = I R_{XY} = 2\times2 = 4\ \mathrm{V}$ (check: the other $12-4 = 8\ \mathrm{V}$ is across the $4\ \Omega$ resistor, $2\times4=8$). **Answer: B.**

questions.enonce_markdown: A cell has an emf of $2.5\ \mathrm{V}$. It cannot be balanced on a potentiometer of length $100.0\ \mathrm{cm}$ when connected to a driver cell of $2.0\ \mathrm{V}$. Which of the following best explains why there is no balance point?
questions.corrige_markdown: A balance point is found where the p.d. along the slide wire equals the emf of the cell being measured. The driver cell supplies at most $2.0\ \mathrm{V}$ across the whole $100.0\ \mathrm{cm}$ wire, so no point on the wire can have a p.d. of $2.5\ \mathrm{V}$ relative to the end. The cause is that the **p.d. across the wire is smaller than the emf to be measured**. A only names a way of getting a small p.d. (a small current gives a small p.d. along the wire), not the reason itself; B is wrong because the balance point would lie beyond the end of the wire, so a short length is not the problem; C is wrong because the cell emf of $2.5\ \mathrm{V}$ is too high for this set-up, not too low. **Answer: D.**

choix.texte: The current in the wire is too low.
The balance length is too small.
The emf of the cell is too low.
The voltage across the wire is too low.

questions.enonce_markdown:
An electrically charged pith ball of mass $4.0\times10^{-4}\ \mathrm{kg}$ is suspended by a light thread of negligible mass and placed in a uniform electric field of strength $4.0\times10^{2}\ \mathrm{N\,C^{-1}}$. If the ball is deflected through an angle of $10^\circ$ then the magnitude of the charge on it is:

*Options as printed:* A) $2.0\ \mathrm{C}$   B) $2.0\times10^{-6}\ \mathrm{C}$   C) $2.0\times10^{-4}\ \mathrm{C}$   D) $2.0\times10^{6}\ \mathrm{C}$
questions.corrige_markdown:
The ball is in equilibrium under three forces: weight $mg$ (down), the electric force $qE$ (horizontal) and the tension $T$.

$T\sin\theta = qE$ and $T\cos\theta = mg$, so $\tan\theta = \dfrac{qE}{mg}$ and

$q = \dfrac{mg\tan\theta}{E} = \dfrac{4.0\times10^{-4}\times9.8\times\tan10^\circ}{4.0\times10^{2}} = 1.7\times10^{-6}\ \mathrm{C}$

(with $g = 10\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$: $1.76\times10^{-6}\ \mathrm{C}$). The exact value $1.7\times10^{-6}\ \mathrm{C}$ is not among the printed options: the nearest one, B ($2.0\times10^{-6}\ \mathrm{C}$), is about 15 % too large, and the others are wrong by orders of magnitude.

**Intended answer: B ($2.0\times10^{-6}\ \mathrm{C}$).**

The printed question is not reliable enough to be marked automatically so it is left open for self-assessment instead of being auto-marked.

questions.enonce_markdown: The resonant frequency in an $L$-$C$ circuit is $40\ \mathrm{MHz}$. When the inductance is increased by a factor of four keeping the capacitance constant, which of the following is the correct value for the new resonant frequency in MHz?
questions.corrige_markdown: $f_0 = \dfrac{1}{2\pi\sqrt{LC}}$, so $f_0 \propto \dfrac{1}{\sqrt L}$. With $L' = 4L$: $f_0' = \dfrac{f_0}{\sqrt4} = \dfrac{40}{2} = 20\ \mathrm{MHz}$. **Answer: B.**

questions.enonce_markdown: Which other essential information is required to calculate the energy needed to change $0.5\ \mathrm{kg}$ of ice at $-10\ ^\circ\mathrm{C}$ to water at $20\ ^\circ\mathrm{C}$ if energy lost to the surroundings and calorimeter is negligible.

choix.texte: Mass of water, Specific latent heat of fusion of ice and Specific heat capacity of water
mass of calorimeter, Specific heat capacity of water and Specific latent heat of fusion of ice
Specific heat capacity of ice, Specific latent heat of fusion of ice, Specific heat capacity of water
Specific heat capacity of ice, Temperature rise, Specific latent heat of fusion of ice and Time taken

questions.enonce_markdown:
The simple kinetic theory of gases may be used to derive the expression relating the pressure $P$ to the density $\rho$ of a gas.

$$p=\frac{1}{3}\rho\overline{c^{2}}$$

In this expression, what does $\overline{c^{2}}$ represent?
questions.corrige_markdown: $\overline{c^2}$ is the **mean square speed**: take the square of each molecular speed, then average. It is not the square of the mean speed ($\bar c^{\,2}$, option B), and the root-mean-square speed is $c_{rms}=\sqrt{\overline{c^2}}$ (option C). **Answer: D.**

choix.texte: The square of the most probable speed of the gas molecule
The square of the average speed of the gas molecules
The root-mean square speed of the gas molecules
The average of the squares of the speeds of the gas molecules

questions.enonce_markdown:
![fig-2](gce-al-physics-2019-p1-officiel-cameroun_exercice_1_fig_2.png)

Figure 2 shows a ray of light $X$ in glass refracted into air. If the speed of light in air is $3.0\times10^{8}\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$, which of the following is the correct value for the speed of light in glass?
questions.corrige_markdown:
The marked angles ($65^\circ$ and $51^\circ$) are measured from the **surface** (the horizontal line), not from the normal $NN'$. So the angles to the normal are

- in glass: $i = 90^\circ - 65^\circ = 25^\circ$,
- in air: $r = 90^\circ - 51^\circ = 39^\circ$ (larger, as expected for light leaving glass).

Snell's law: $n_{glass}\sin25^\circ = n_{air}\sin39^\circ$, so $n_{glass} = \dfrac{\sin39^\circ}{\sin25^\circ} = 1.49$.

$v_{glass} = \dfrac{c}{n} = \dfrac{3.0\times10^{8}}{1.49} = 2.0\times10^{8}\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$. (Taking $65^\circ$ and $51^\circ$ from the normal would give $n<1$, impossible.) **Answer: A.**

questions.enonce_markdown: Tungsten obeys Ohm's law because
questions.corrige_markdown: Ohm's law: the current through a conductor is proportional to the p.d. across it **provided the temperature (and other physical conditions) stay constant**. Option C is that statement. A tungsten filament lamp does not follow it over a wide range because heating raises the resistance, but at constant temperature $I \propto V$. A describes the lamp's behaviour, not a reason for obeying the law; B and D are not statements of Ohm's law ($R$ is not proportional to $T$ in Celsius). **Answer: C.**

choix.texte: the current decreases with increase in temperature.
the current in it is proportional to the number of charge carriers.
the current through it is proportional to the p.d. across it at constant temperature.
the resistance is proportional to temperature.

questions.enonce_markdown:
A diffraction grating of $500$ lines per millimetre is illuminated normally by light of wavelength $600\ \mathrm{nm}$. Which of the following images can be seen on either side of the normal excluding the central image?

*Options as printed:* A) 3   B) 4   C) 6   D) 2
questions.corrige_markdown:
Grating spacing: $d = \dfrac{1}{500}\ \mathrm{mm} = 2.0\times10^{-6}\ \mathrm{m}$. The condition $n\lambda = d\sin\theta$ needs $\sin\theta\le1$, so

$n \le \dfrac{d}{\lambda} = \dfrac{2.0\times10^{-6}}{600\times10^{-9}} = 3.33$, i.e. $n = 1, 2, 3$ (angles $17.5^\circ$, $36.9^\circ$, $64.2^\circ$).

So **3 orders** are seen on each side of the central image, **6 images** in all. The wording "on either side" does not say whether the count is per side (option A, 3) or for both sides together (option C, 6), so the question is left open.



The printed question is not reliable enough to be marked automatically so it is left open for self-assessment instead of being auto-marked.

questions.enonce_markdown:
![fig-3](gce-al-physics-2019-p1-officiel-cameroun_exercice_1_fig_3.png)

Figure 3 shows the variation of $1/f$ against $L$, where $f$ is the frequency of a tuning fork and $L$ is the length of the vibrating air column. The end correction is $c$, and the velocity of sound in air is $v$.
questions.corrige_markdown:
For the fundamental resonance of a column closed at one end, $L + c = \dfrac{\lambda}{4} = \dfrac{v}{4f}$, so

$\dfrac{1}{f} = \dfrac{4}{v}L + \dfrac{4c}{v}$.

- Slope $= \dfrac{4}{v}$, hence $v = \dfrac{4}{\text{slope}}$ (C is true; A is false).
- Intercept on the $1/f$ axis (the length $XY$) is $\dfrac{4c}{v}$, not $\dfrac{c}{v}$ (D false) and not the end correction (B false).
- The end correction $c$ is the (negative) intercept on the $L$ axis, the length $ZY$.

**Answer: C.**

choix.texte: The slope of the graph is $4c/v$
The speed of sound in air is $4/\text{slope}$.
The intercept of the graph is $c/v$

questions.enonce_markdown: The first law of thermodynamics for an ideal gas may be stated in the form $\Delta U = \Delta Q + \Delta W$. Which of the following is the most correct statement about the equation?
questions.corrige_markdown:
The internal energy of an ideal gas depends only on its temperature. At constant temperature $\Delta U = 0$, whatever heat is supplied (it all becomes work done by the gas): D is true.

- A: if the temperature rises, $\Delta U>0$, so $\Delta Q \neq -\Delta W$.
- B: with no heat flow (adiabatic) $\Delta U = \Delta W \neq 0$ in general.
- C: in the form $\Delta U = \Delta Q + \Delta W$, $\Delta W$ is the work done **on** the gas.

**Answer: D.**

choix.texte: $\Delta Q = -\Delta W$ when the temperature increases slightly.
$\Delta U = 0$ when no heat enters or leaves the system.
$\Delta W$ is the work done by the gas
$\Delta U = 0$ when the heat is supplied at constant temperature

questions.enonce_markdown: Two bodies $P$ and $Q$ are in thermal equilibrium. This statement means that
questions.corrige_markdown: Two bodies are in thermal equilibrium when they are at the same temperature, so there is no **net** transfer of thermal energy between them (the exchange is equal in both directions). A is the best statement. B is wrong (the net rate is zero, not just constant), C is wrong (internal energy depends on mass and heat capacity as well as temperature) and D is wrong (bodies can be in equilibrium without touching, for example through radiation). **Answer: A.**

choix.texte: There is no transfer of energy between P and Q.
The rate of transfer of heat between P and Q is constant.
P and Q have the same amount of internal energy.
P and Q are in physical contact with each other.

questions.enonce_markdown: An electron moves in a circular orbit in a uniform $B$-field. Which of the following statements is the most correct?
questions.corrige_markdown:
The magnetic force provides the centripetal force: $Bev = \dfrac{mv^2}{r}$, so $r = \dfrac{mv}{Be}$ and the period is $T = \dfrac{2\pi r}{v} = \dfrac{2\pi m}{Be}$, which does not contain $v$: A is true.

B is false (the force is perpendicular to the field and to the velocity), C is false ($v = Ber/m$ grows with $r$) and D is false ($B = mv/er$, so $B \propto 1/r$). **Answer: A.**

choix.texte: The period of the electron in the orbit is independent of the speed of the electron.
The force on the electron is parallel to the field
The speed of the electron is independent of the radius of the orbit.
The B-field is proportional to the radius of the circle.

questions.enonce_markdown:
![fig-4](gce-al-physics-2019-p1-officiel-cameroun_exercice_1_fig_4.png)

Figure 4 shows how the force exerted normally on a vertical wall by a fast moving tennis ball varies with time. Which of the following statements is correct about the interaction?
questions.corrige_markdown:
The area under a force-time graph is the impulse $\int F\,dt$, and impulse equals the change of momentum (the wall exerts on the ball a force equal and opposite to the one in the graph, so the magnitude of the change of momentum of the ball is this area). A is correct.

Time runs to the right, so contact begins at $X$ and ends at $Y$ (B is false). The maximum force is at $N$, not at $X$ where the force is zero (C is false), and impulse is an area, not a quantity with a minimum at a point (D is false). **Answer: A.**

choix.texte: The area under the graph gives the change in momentum experienced by the ball.
The contact of the ball with the wall begins at Y and ends at X.
The maximum pressure on the ball is X.
The minimum impulse on the ball is at N.

questions.enonce_markdown: The work function of caesium is $1.4\ \mathrm{eV}$. The maximum velocity of electrons emitted from the surface of caesium when illuminated by ultra violet light of wavelength $380\ \mathrm{nm}$ is:
questions.corrige_markdown:
Photon energy: $E = \dfrac{hc}{\lambda} = \dfrac{6.63\times10^{-34}\times3.00\times10^{8}}{380\times10^{-9}} = 5.23\times10^{-19}\ \mathrm{J} = 3.27\ \mathrm{eV}$.

Einstein's equation: $E_{k,max} = hf - \phi = 3.27 - 1.4 = 1.87\ \mathrm{eV} = 1.87\times1.60\times10^{-19} = 2.99\times10^{-19}\ \mathrm{J}$.

$v_{max} = \sqrt{\dfrac{2E_k}{m_e}} = \sqrt{\dfrac{2\times2.99\times10^{-19}}{9.11\times10^{-31}}} = 8.1\times10^{5}\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$. **Answer: A.**

questions.enonce_markdown: Which of the following statements best explains the fact that electromagnetic radiation and electrons can both exhibit wave-like characteristics?
questions.corrige_markdown:
Diffraction (and interference) is the characteristic behaviour of waves. Electrons of suitable energy and X-rays both show diffraction patterns when they pass through crystals, because their wavelengths are comparable to the atomic spacing ($\sim10^{-10}\ \mathrm{m}$). This shows that both radiation and electrons behave as waves: B.

A is about particle behaviour, C is false (radio waves are not refracted by crystals in that way) and D concerns only electromagnetic radiation, not electrons. **Answer: B.**

choix.texte: Electrons have light mass and move in a circular path in a B-field.
Electrons and X-rays are both diffracted by crystals.
Electrons and radio waves can be both reflected and refracted by crystals.
Gamma and x-rays can be refracted and diffracted by crystals.

questions.enonce_markdown: When boron-11 (${}^{11}_{5}B$) is bombarded with alpha particles a new nucleus is formed and a neutron is released. Which of the nuclear equations below represents the reaction?
questions.corrige_markdown:
An alpha particle is a helium-4 nucleus, ${}^{4}_{2}He$. Conservation of nucleon number: $11+4 = 15 = 14+1$; conservation of charge (proton number): $5+2 = 7 = 7+0$, and proton number 7 is nitrogen. A balances: ${}^{14}_{7}N$.

B has a nonsensical proton number (76) and carbon would not balance the charge. C uses deuterium (not an alpha) and labels $Z=6$ as N. D balances numerically but uses ${}^{3}_{2}He$, which is not an alpha particle. **Answer: A.**

![fig-5](gce-al-physics-2019-p1-officiel-cameroun_exercice_1_fig_5.png)

Figure 5 shows how the applied force, $F$, varies with the extension, $x$, for two different materials $P$ and $Q$. Which of the following combinations best identifies the materials $P$ and $Q$?

| | P | Q |
|---|---|---|
| A | Rubber | Copper |
| B | Rubber | Glass |
| C | Glass | Rubber |
| D | Iron | Glass |
questions.corrige_markdown:
$P$ is a steep straight line through the origin: the material obeys Hooke's law up to fracture and is stiff and brittle, which fits glass (or iron). $Q$ is a curve that is easily stretched at first, flattens, then stiffens again: the characteristic S-shaped curve of rubber.

A is wrong ($P$ would not be rubber), B has the same fault, D is wrong ($Q$ would not be glass, which is linear and brittle). Only C pairs a stiff linear $P$ (glass) with a rubber-like $Q$. **Answer: C.**

questions.enonce_markdown: When light falls on a clean glass block of refractive index $1.5$, it is noticed using a Polaroid that the refracted ray is completely plane polarized. Which of the following values is the angle of reflection?
questions.corrige_markdown: Complete plane polarisation occurs at the Brewster (polarising) angle $\theta_p$, given by $\tan\theta_p = n = 1.5$, so $\theta_p = 56.3^\circ \approx 56^\circ$. At this angle the reflected and refracted rays are at $90^\circ$ to each other ($56.3^\circ + 33.7^\circ = 90^\circ$). The angle of reflection equals the angle of incidence, $56^\circ$. (Strictly it is the **reflected** ray that is completely polarised; the printed wording says refracted, but the numerical answer is unaffected.) **Answer: A.**

questions.enonce_markdown:
![fig-6](gce-al-physics-2019-p1-officiel-cameroun_exercice_1_fig_6.png)

Figure 6 shows a metal rule of mass $200\ \mathrm{g}$ supported by a pivot at the $20\ \mathrm{cm}$ mark and a string at the $100\ \mathrm{cm}$ mark. The string passes round a frictionless pulley and carries a mass of $80\ \mathrm{g}$.

At which mark on the rule must a $20\ \mathrm{g}$ mass be suspended so that the rule balances?
questions.corrige_markdown:
Take moments about the pivot (the $20\ \mathrm{cm}$ mark). Use weights in "gram-force" (the factor $g$ cancels). The rule is uniform, so its weight acts at its centre, the $50\ \mathrm{cm}$ mark, $30\ \mathrm{cm}$ to the right of the pivot.

- Clockwise: weight of the rule $200\times30 = 6000\ \mathrm{g\,cm}$.
- Anticlockwise: the string goes up over the pulley, so it pulls **up** on the right end with a force equal to the weight of $80\ \mathrm{g}$, at $80\ \mathrm{cm}$ from the pivot: $80\times80 = 6400\ \mathrm{g\,cm}$.

The net moment is $400\ \mathrm{g\,cm}$ anticlockwise, so the $20\ \mathrm{g}$ mass must give a clockwise moment of $400\ \mathrm{g\,cm}$ on the right of the pivot: $20\,d = 400$, $d = 20\ \mathrm{cm}$. The mark is $20+20 = 40\ \mathrm{cm}$. **Answer: B.**

questions.enonce_markdown: Which of the following quantities has the smallest numerical values in SI units?
questions.corrige_markdown: In SI units: electron charge $1.6\times10^{-19}\ \mathrm{C}$; electron mass $9.1\times10^{-31}\ \mathrm{kg}$; alpha particle mass $6.6\times10^{-27}\ \mathrm{kg}$; hydrogen atom mass $1.7\times10^{-27}\ \mathrm{kg}$. The smallest number is the mass of an electron. **Answer: B.**

choix.texte: The mass of an alpha particle.
The mass of a hydrogen atom.

questions.enonce_markdown: The electrons in a cathode ray tube are accelerated from the cathode to the anode by a potential difference, $V$. This p.d. is increased by a factor of 4. Which of the following statements is true when the electrons arrive at the screen?
questions.corrige_markdown: The work done on the electron is $eV = \tfrac12 m v^2$. So $E_k \propto V$ (four times) and $v = \sqrt{2eV/m} \propto \sqrt V$ (two times). The momentum $p = mv$ also doubles, so D is false. **Answer: B.**

choix.texte: It will have four times the kinetic energy and four times its velocity.
It will have four times the kinetic energy and two times the velocity
It will have twice the kinetic energy and velocity
It will have the same momentum in both cases.

questions.enonce_markdown:
Which of the following descriptions is consistent with a constant decrease in the current through a uniform piece of a conductor?

| | No of electrons per unit volume | Drift velocity of electrons |
|---|---|---|
| A | Unaltered | Increases |
| B | Decreases | unaltered |
| C | Unaltered | Decreases |
| D | Increases | Decreases |

*Options as printed:* A) A   B) B   C) C   D) D
questions.corrige_markdown:
The current is $I = nAvq$. For a uniform conductor of fixed cross-section $A$ and fixed charge $q$, $I$ falls if $n$ falls at constant $v$, or if $v$ falls at constant $n$.

- A: $I$ increases, so no.
- B: $n$ decreases, $v$ constant: $I$ decreases, consistent.
- C: $n$ constant, $v$ decreases: $I$ decreases, consistent.
- D: $n$ rises while $v$ falls: the effect on $I$ is not determined.

B and C both fit. C is the physically natural one, since in a given piece of metal $n$ is fixed by the material, but the question does not say so, so it is left open for self-assessment.

questions.enonce_markdown:
A converging lens of focal length $12.0\ \mathrm{cm}$ forms an upright image four times the size of its real image. Which of the following is the distance of the object?

*Options as printed:* A) $15\ \mathrm{cm}$   B) $30\ \mathrm{cm}$   C) $12\ \mathrm{cm}$   D) $24\ \mathrm{cm}$
questions.corrige_markdown:
The statement is garbled: a real image is never upright. Two readings:

- Real image four times the size of the object ($v = 4u$): $\dfrac1u + \dfrac1{4u} = \dfrac1{12}$, so $\dfrac{5}{4u} = \dfrac1{12}$ and $u = 15\ \mathrm{cm}$ (option A).
- Upright (virtual) image four times the size of the object ($|v| = 4u$): $\dfrac1u - \dfrac1{4u} = \dfrac1{12}$, so $u = 9\ \mathrm{cm}$, which is not among the options.

Only the first reading matches an option, so the intended answer is A ($15\ \mathrm{cm}$).

**Intended answer: A ($15\ \mathrm{cm}$).**

The printed question is not reliable enough to be marked automatically so it is left open for self-assessment instead of being auto-marked.

questions.enonce_markdown: Which of the following statements best explains why an ammeter is always connected in series in an electrical circuit?

It is designed with a very low resistance so that the p.d. across it is negligible and it does not alter the current it measures. That is what makes series connection acceptable: C. A is true of any component, and B and D are not reasons. **Answer: C.**

choix.texte: It allows current to flow through it.
The ammeter is a very accurate current measuring instrument.
The pd across the ammeter is usually negligible.
The ammeter is extremely sensitive to changes in temperature.

questions.enonce_markdown: In a number of successive decay processes in a nucleus there is a net decrease in the proton number by one and a net decrease in the nucleon number by four. Which of the following particles could be emitted?
questions.corrige_markdown:
An alpha particle lowers the nucleon number by 4 and the proton number by 2. A beta-minus particle raises the proton number by 1 and leaves the nucleon number unchanged.

- 1 alpha + 1 beta: nucleon number $-4$, proton number $-2+1 = -1$. This is the required change.
- 1 alpha + 2 beta: proton number change $0$. 1 alpha + 3 beta: $+1$.
- 2 alpha + 1 beta: nucleon number $-8$.

**Answer: A.**

choix.texte: An alpha and a beta particle.

questions.enonce_markdown:
In an experiment to determine the heat capacity of a metal heat was supplied at a steady rate of $1000\ \mathrm{J\,s^{-1}}$.

![fig-7](gce-al-physics-2019-p1-officiel-cameroun_exercice_1_fig_7.png)

Figure 7 shows the variation of temperature with time. If the mass of the metal is $7.5\ \mathrm{kg}$, then the value for the specific heat capacity of the metal would be:
questions.corrige_markdown:
Energy supplied per second: $P = 1000\ \mathrm{J\,s^{-1}}$ (no loss assumed). Then $P = mc\dfrac{\Delta\theta}{\Delta t}$.

Gradient of the graph: the line passes through the origin and through $(8\ \mathrm{s},\ 20\ ^\circ\mathrm{C})$ (and $(4,\ 10)$), so $\dfrac{\Delta\theta}{\Delta t} = 2.5\ ^\circ\mathrm{C\,s^{-1}}$.

$c = \dfrac{P}{m\times\text{gradient}} = \dfrac{1000}{7.5\times2.5} = 53.3\ \mathrm{J\,kg^{-1}\,K^{-1}}$.

The other options correspond to gradients of $0.4$, $0.044$ and $0.071\ ^\circ\mathrm{C\,s^{-1}}$, which the graph does not show. **Answer: B.**

questions.enonce_markdown: A moving-coil galvanometer of internal resistance $20\ \Omega$ gives a full-scale deflection for a current of $10.0\times10^{-3}\ \mathrm{A}$. If an external resistor of resistance $0.025\ \Omega$ is connected in parallel to it, this instrument can be used as a voltmeter or ammeter of range:
questions.corrige_markdown:
A resistor in parallel is a shunt, which makes an **ammeter** of larger range (a voltmeter would need a series resistor).

At full scale the p.d. across the galvanometer is $V = 10.0\times10^{-3}\times20 = 0.20\ \mathrm{V}$. The shunt carries $I_s = \dfrac{0.20}{0.025} = 8.0\ \mathrm{A}$. Total current: $8.0 + 0.010 = 8.01\ \mathrm{A} \approx 8.0\ \mathrm{A}$. Range $0$-$8.0\ \mathrm{A}$. **Answer: C.**

questions.enonce_markdown: An observer is moving towards a sound source of constant frequency with a velocity of $40\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$. He observes the frequency to be $560\ \mathrm{Hz}$. If the velocity at which the observer is moving towards the sound source doubles, what will be the new observed frequency? (speed of sound in air is $330\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$)
questions.corrige_markdown:
For an observer moving towards a stationary source: $f' = f_0\dfrac{v + v_o}{v}$.

First case: $560 = f_0\times\dfrac{330+40}{330}$, so $f_0 = 560\times\dfrac{330}{370} = 499.5\ \mathrm{Hz}$.

Second case ($v_o = 80\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$): $f' = 499.5\times\dfrac{330+80}{330} = 620.5\ \mathrm{Hz} \approx 620\ \mathrm{Hz}$. **Answer: A.**

questions.enonce_markdown:
![fig-8](gce-al-physics-2019-p1-officiel-cameroun_exercice_1_fig_8.png)

Figure 8 shows a book lying on a box which rests on a table. A free-body force diagram for the box is also shown. Which of the following statements is/are correct?

1. $Q$ is the pull of the earth on the box
2. $P$ is the push on the box by the ground.
3. $R$ is the pull of the earth on the box.
questions.corrige_markdown:
In the free-body diagram of the box, the arrows show where each force acts:

- $P$ points up from the bottom face: the upward (normal) contact force of the table (the "ground") on the box.
- $Q$ points down from the top face: the contact force of the book on the box.
- $R$ points down from the centre of the box: its weight, the pull of the earth on the box.

Statement 1 is false ($Q$ is the push of the book, not the earth's pull), statements 2 and 3 are true. **Answer: B.**

questions.enonce_markdown:
A parallel plate capacitor is connected in series with a battery. Which of the following procedures would result in doubling the capacitance of the capacitor?

| | Area | Distance between the plates |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Increasing area by 4 | Half the distance |
| 2 | Keep area constant | Increase distance by 4 |
| 3 | Half area | Increase distance by 4 |

*Options as printed:* A) 1 and 2 are correct   B) 2 and 3 are correct   C) 1 only is correct   D) 3 only is correct

$C = \dfrac{\varepsilon A}{d}$.

1. Area $\times4$, distance $\times\tfrac12$: $C$ becomes $8C$.
2. Area unchanged, distance $\times4$: $C$ becomes $\tfrac14 C$.
3. Area $\times\tfrac12$, distance $\times4$: $C$ becomes $\tfrac18 C$.

None of the three procedures doubles the capacitance, and the answer options have no "none correct" choice. The printed table is therefore faulty (for example "double the distance" in row 1 would give $2C$), and the question is left open.

questions.enonce_markdown:
The entropy of a thermodynamic system in equilibrium is

1. zero
2. Always increasing
3. Always decreasing

*Options as printed:* A) 1 and 2 are correct   B) 2 and 3 are correct   C) 1 only is correct   D) 3 only is correct
questions.corrige_markdown:
For an isolated system, entropy increases in any spontaneous process until the system reaches equilibrium; at equilibrium the entropy is at its **maximum value and constant**. It is therefore not always increasing (2), not always decreasing (3), and not zero (1): entropy is zero only for a perfect crystal at absolute zero. None of the three statements is correct and no "none correct" option is offered, so the question is left open.

questions.enonce_markdown:
Which of the following deductions is/are true for Newton's first law of motion?

1. A body is in uniform motion only when no force acts on it.
2. A resultant force is necessary to cause an object to accelerate
3. The motion of a body in the absent of a net force is rectilinear.
questions.corrige_markdown:
Newton's first law: a body stays at rest or in uniform motion in a straight line unless a resultant (net) force acts on it.

- 1: false as written. A body can be in uniform motion with several forces acting, provided they balance (zero **resultant** force).
- 2: true. With no resultant force there is no acceleration, so acceleration needs a resultant force.
- 3: true. With zero net force the velocity is constant, so the path is a straight line (or the body is at rest).

**Answer: B.**

questions.enonce_markdown:
![fig-9](gce-al-physics-2019-p1-officiel-cameroun_exercice_1_fig_9.png)

Figure 9 shows two infinitely long conductors $X$ and $Y$ of negligible cross-sectional area placed $1.0\ \mathrm{m}$ apart in a vacuum. If the force per unit length between the conductors is $8.0\times10^{-7}\ \mathrm{N\,m^{-1}}$, then it can be concluded that:

1. The current flowing in each of the conductor is $2\ \mathrm{A}$.
2. The force between the conductor is attractive
3. The current flowing in each of the conductor is $4\ \mathrm{A}$
questions.corrige_markdown:
Both arrows in the figure point the same way, so the currents are parallel and the wires **attract** each other (statement 2 true).

Force per unit length: $\dfrac{F}{L} = \dfrac{\mu_0 I_1 I_2}{2\pi d} = \dfrac{2\times10^{-7}\,I_1I_2}{1.0}$, so $I_1 I_2 = \dfrac{8.0\times10^{-7}}{2\times10^{-7}} = 4\ \mathrm{A^2}$.

For equal currents ("the current in each of the conductor"), $I = 2\ \mathrm{A}$ (statement 1 true). Statement 3 would give $I_1I_2 = 16\ \mathrm{A^2}$, false. (Strictly only the product $I_1I_2$ is fixed; equal currents are assumed by the wording.) **Answer: A.**

questions.enonce_markdown:
The displacement of a particle undergoing simple harmonic motion is given by $x = 8\sin(100t)$, where $x$ is measured in cm. Which of the following statement is correct?

1. the frequency of oscillation is $16\ \mathrm{Hz}$
2. The velocity is given by $v = 800\cos(100t)$
3. The displacement after is $8\ \mathrm{cm}$
questions.corrige_markdown:
Compare with $x = A\sin\omega t$: $A = 8\ \mathrm{cm}$ and $\omega = 100\ \mathrm{rad\,s^{-1}}$.

1. $f = \dfrac{\omega}{2\pi} = \dfrac{100}{2\pi} = 15.9\ \mathrm{Hz} \approx 16\ \mathrm{Hz}$: true.
2. $v = \dfrac{dx}{dt} = 8\times100\cos(100t) = 800\cos(100t)$ (in $\mathrm{cm\,s^{-1}}$): true.
3. As printed the statement is incomplete ("The displacement after is 8 cm"). The displacement equals $8\ \mathrm{cm}$ only at certain instants (it is the amplitude), so it cannot be a correct general statement. It is also impossible for 1, 2 and 3 to be all true as no option offers it.

The only option containing 1 and 2 is A. **Answer: A.**

questions.enonce_markdown:
The wavelength of light emitted by a Helium-Neon laser is $6.33\times10^{-7}\ \mathrm{m}$. Which of the following is/are correct?

1. The light is emitted when electron are pumped up to higher energy level
2. The light is monochromatic because all the photons have the same wavelength.
3. They corresponds to a photon of $1.96\ \mathrm{eV}$.
questions.corrige_markdown:
1. False: pumping raises electrons to a higher level (absorption). Light is emitted when electrons drop to a lower level (stimulated emission).
2. True: all the photons have the same wavelength, so the light is monochromatic.
3. True: $E = \dfrac{hc}{\lambda} = \dfrac{6.63\times10^{-34}\times3.00\times10^{8}}{6.33\times10^{-7}} = 3.14\times10^{-19}\ \mathrm{J} = \dfrac{3.14\times10^{-19}}{1.60\times10^{-19}} = 1.96\ \mathrm{eV}$.

**Answer: B.**

questions.enonce_markdown:
A dielectric increases the capacitance of a capacitor by

1. Increasing the strength of the electric field between the plates of the capacitor.
2. Drawing electrons off the negative plate to the positive plate.
3. Reducing the potential difference between the plates of the capacitor.
questions.corrige_markdown: The molecules of the dielectric become polarised and set up a field opposing the field of the plates. For a given charge $Q$ the net field between the plates is **reduced**, so the p.d. falls, and $C = Q/V$ increases (statement 3 true, statement 1 false). In charging, electrons move from the positive plate to the negative plate (the reverse of statement 2), and this is not how a dielectric acts, so 2 is false. **Answer: D.**

questions.enonce_markdown:
A water pump raises water through a height of $4\ \mathrm{m}$ at the rate of $600\ \mathrm{kg}$ per minute delivering it with a velocity of $10\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$.

1. The increase in potential energy per second is $392\ \mathrm{W}$.
2. The power output of the pump is $892\ \mathrm{W}$
3. The increase in the kinetic energy is $2.5\times10^{4}\ \mathrm{J}$
questions.corrige_markdown:
Mass raised per second: $\dfrac{600}{60} = 10\ \mathrm{kg\,s^{-1}}$ (with $g = 9.8\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$).

1. Potential energy gained per second: $10\times9.8\times4 = 392\ \mathrm{W}$: true.
2. Kinetic energy gained per second: $\tfrac12\times10\times10^{2} = 500\ \mathrm{W}$. Output power $= 392 + 500 = 892\ \mathrm{W}$: true.
3. The kinetic energy gain is $500\ \mathrm{J}$ each second, i.e. $3.0\times10^{4}\ \mathrm{J}$ per minute. Neither equals $2.5\times10^{4}\ \mathrm{J}$: false.

**Answer: A.**

questions.enonce_markdown:
A cell of e.m.f $9.0\ \mathrm{V}$ and negligible internal resistance is connected in series with a $50\ \Omega$ resistor, $R$, using very thin resistance wire of resistance per unit length of $4.0\ \Omega$ per unit length. The circuit is shown in figure 10.

![fig-10](gce-al-physics-2019-p1-officiel-cameroun_exercice_1_fig_10.png)

Which of these is/are true?

1. $a$ is at a lower potential than $b$.
2. $b$ is at a higher potential than $c$
3. $a$ is at a higher potential than $c$
questions.corrige_markdown:
The cell symbol has its long plate (the positive terminal) on the side of $a$, and its short plate (negative) joined to $c$ by a plain wire. The switch in the figure is drawn open.

With the switch open no current flows, so there is no p.d. across $R$: $a$ and $b$ are at the same potential (statement 1 false), and both are $9.0\ \mathrm{V}$ above $c$ (statements 2 and 3 true).

With the switch closed the current flows from the positive terminal through $R$ ($a$ to $b$) and then back to $c$, and the potential falls all the way round: $a$ is above $b$ (statement 1 still false), $b$ is above $c$ and $a$ is above $c$. The answer is the same in both cases. **Answer: B.**

questions.corrige_markdown:

Of the two decreasing curves, B starts away from the $y$-axis (as for $x$ measured from the centre, where the curve starts at $r = R$) and C starts on the $y$-axis but looks like an infinite $1/x$ divergence. Neither shows exactly a finite value at $x = 0$ for a distance from the surface, so the printed question is ambiguous (B is probably the intended graph) and it is left open.
